summary: An update from BBN on the attempt to release IMPSYS 2600 on May 15, 1972, which failed. The main causes were that the network had grown too large to coordinate operator action at every site, and that IMPs running the old and new systems disturbed each other. BBN planned new attempts. It was replaced by RFC 359.

eli5.summary: The grown-ups tried to switch every machine to new software on the same day and it did not work, because the old and new versions confused each other. They promised to try again with a better plan.

questions: why did the impsys 2600 release fail
subtitle: News about a failed software upgrade and the plan to try again.

tldr.problem: BBN tried to upgrade the IMPSYS software on all network IMPs simultaneously on May 15, 1972, but the upgrade failed because the network had grown too large to coordinate.
tldr.mechanism: The failure happened because old and new systems running side by side interfered with each other, and coordinating operator actions across all sites proved impossible. BBN scheduled new attempts for later dates.
tldr.outcome: This early incident showed the challenges of managing distributed systems and coordinating changes across many independent sites.

today: RFC 343 is a historic record replaced by RFC 359. It documents an early operational crisis that drove lessons about coordinating changes in distributed systems.

sections.title: The Failed Release
sections.content:
On May 15, 1972, BBN attempted to release IMPSYS 2600, a new version of the IMP operating system, across the entire ARPANET. The upgrade failed. The primary reasons were operational rather than software bugs: the network had grown too large to successfully coordinate operator intervention at all sites simultaneously.

An unexpected problem made this worse: IMPs running the old system interfered with adjacent IMPs running the new system, and vice versa, which the authors called the poisoning effect. This extended the release process much longer than anticipated.
sections.eli5: When they tried to switch every machine to new software, the network was too big to coordinate. Also, old machines confused new machines next to them on the network.

sections.title: Coordination Instructions
sections.content:
To prepare for the next attempt, BBN asked all sites with Model 516 IMPs to set specific hardware switches in standby mode: HALT INH (off), W.D.T. (off), AUTO RSTRT (on), and MEMORY PRTCT (off). Sites were told not to use the IMP's Trace routine during the release day, and Terminal IMPs could be turned off temporarily.

BBN scheduled the next attempt for Wednesday, May 31, and then every Tuesday thereafter (June 6, 13, 20, and so on) until the release succeeded. Sites should avoid scheduling production work during the release window.
sections.eli5: BBN asked each site to flip switches on their machines and be ready to help. They would try again on May 31 and keep trying every Tuesday until it worked.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: This RFC was replaced by RFC 359. It documents a critical early challenge in managing the growing ARPANET: coordinating system changes across many independent operators.
sections.eli5: This note got replaced by a later one, but it shows that even in 1972, changing software across a whole network was hard.

references.text: McKenzie, A., "IMP System Change Notification", RFC 359, August 1972.
